disclaimer: This report is for educational and wellness purposes only. It is not a medical diagnosis and does not replace advice from a qualified healthcare professional. HbA1c results should be confirmed by your doctor. Do not start, stop or change any medication without medical advice.

status.label: In the prediabetes range
status.explanation: Your HbA1c is between 5.7% and 6.4%, the range used for prediabetes. This is a common and often reversible stage where lifestyle changes make the biggest difference.

summary: Your HbA1c is in the prediabetes range, which means this is a good time to make changes before things progress further. Your BMI falls in the obese range, and combined with low physical activity and existing fatty liver disease, these factors raise your risk for blood sugar and liver issues. The most valuable next steps are keeping up with your highlighted liver and HbA1c checks, building in regular physical activity, and following your food plan, including completely avoiding alcohol and cutting added sugars. Small, steady changes can make a real difference over time.

risk_factors.label: Existing health condition: Fatty liver disease

comorbidity_assessment.note: Fatty liver can make it harder for your body to manage blood sugar properly, and higher blood sugar levels can in turn add more strain to the liver. Monitoring liver health closely and reducing fat around the liver through weight loss can help both concerns together.

constraints: Cut added sugars and sugary drinks, especially fructose-sweetened ones.

foods_to_eat: Whole grains like brown rice, millets (ragi, jowar, bajra)
Pulses and legumes such as moong dal, chana, rajma
Non-starchy vegetables like spinach, lauki, cucumber, tomato
Low-fat dairy such as curd and buttermilk in small portions
Nuts and seeds in small handfuls
High-fibre fruits like guava, papaya, and apple in moderation
Herbs and spices like turmeric, cumin, and fenugreek
foods_to_avoid: Sugary drinks, packaged juices, and sodas
Sweets and desserts made with refined sugar
Deep-fried snacks like samosas and pakoras
Refined flour (maida) products such as white bread and naan
Processed and packaged snacks high in salt or sugar
plan.portion_guidance: Use small katoris and bowls to naturally control portions. Fill half your plate with non-starchy vegetables, one quarter with whole grains or millets, and one quarter with dal, paneer, or legumes. Keep roti portions to one small piece per meal and avoid second helpings of rice or roti.
plan.hydration: Drink about 8 to 10 glasses of water through the day. Add unsweetened buttermilk or infused water with cucumber or mint if you want variety. Avoid sugary drinks, packaged juices, and alcohol completely.
based_on: fatty liver disease: low added sugar and low fried food

exercise: Start with 10-15 minutes of brisk walking most days, building slowly over a few weeks
Aim to work up gradually toward at least 150 minutes a week of moderate activity, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming
Add simple muscle-strengthening activities (bodyweight exercises like squats, wall push-ups, or resistance bands) on 2 non-consecutive days each week
Progress slowly given your current sedentary activity level, listening to your body as you build stamina
lifestyle.walking_goal: Begin with 10 minutes of walking daily this week, then gradually build up to 30 minutes a day, at least 5 days a week, over the next 1-2 months
lifestyle.weight_management: Your BMI is in the obese range, and losing 7-10% of your current body weight can substantially improve liver fat and support better blood sugar control. Focus on gradual, sustainable changes such as building more vegetables, whole grains, and legumes into your vegetarian meals, practicing portion awareness, and increasing your daily movement. Small, steady progress over time tends to work better than rapid changes.
lifestyle.sleep: Aim for 7-9 hours of sleep each night. Try to keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, even on weekends. Limit screens for an hour before bed, keep your bedroom cool and dark, and avoid caffeine in the afternoon and evening to help your body wind down.
stress: Practice slow, deep breathing for 5-10 minutes daily, such as inhaling for 4 counts and exhaling for 6 counts
Try progressive muscle relaxation or a short guided meditation before bed to ease tension
Consider gentle yoga or stretching, which can help with both stress and physical activity goals
Make time for activities you enjoy, such as reading, music, or time with family and friends
behaviour_change: Since you drink occasionally, it's best to avoid alcohol completely. Alcohol can worsen fatty liver disease and adds extra calories that make weight management harder, so cutting it out entirely will support your liver health and your HbA1c goals
Build a regular habit of daily movement, even small amounts, to counter long periods of sitting, such as standing or walking for a few minutes every hour
Keep a simple food and activity journal for a few weeks to build awareness of patterns and track your progress
Set small, specific weekly goals (like adding one extra vegetarian meal with more fiber, or walking an extra 5 minutes) rather than trying to change everything at once
Consider connecting with a support group or dietitian experienced in Indian vegetarian diets and fatty liver management for personalized encouragement
based_on: Constraint: weight loss of 7-10% can improve liver fat

monitoring.name: HbA1c
monitoring.why: Catches progression from prediabetes to diabetes early.

monitoring.name: Liver check (liver tests and FIB-4 score)
monitoring.why: Fatty liver is common with diabetes and obesity and can progress without symptoms.
monitoring.frequency: FIB-4 score every 1–2 years, or sooner if your doctor finds a higher risk

monitoring.name: Fasting blood sugar
monitoring.why: Shows your blood glucose after an overnight fast and complements HbA1c.
monitoring.frequency: Alongside your HbA1c test, or as your doctor advises

monitoring.name: Blood pressure
monitoring.why: High blood pressure multiplies the heart and kidney risks of high blood glucose.
monitoring.frequency: At every doctor visit; at home regularly if you have high blood pressure

preventive_actions: Avoid alcohol completely, as recommended for your liver and blood sugar health.
Cut out added sugars and sugary drinks, especially those sweetened with fructose.
Aim to reduce body weight by 7–10%, which research shows can meaningfully improve liver fat.
Add regular physical activity to your routine, even short daily walks, to help counter low activity levels.
Keep up with your highlighted liver tests (including FIB-4 score) and HbA1c checks as scheduled.
Follow your calorie target of 1200 calories per day as part of a vegetarian eating pattern.

hba1c_caveat: HbA1c can be less accurate if you have anaemia, kidney disease, a recent blood transfusion or certain haemoglobin variants.
